teaser.text: Ventas is a real-estate company whose buildings house older people, patients, doctors and researchers. A dollar reaches it either through the operating results of a senior community or as rent from an organization using one of its properties, and then leaves through property costs, corporate bills, financing and investment in buildings.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Ventas?

paragraphs.text: The bear case starts at the guidance low and assumes a 5% per-share decline before earnings flatten. It produces $1,905 million in 2027 and $1,982 million in 2029. The bull starts at the guidance high and assumes 11% per-share growth before slowing to 10%, reaching $2,918 million in 2029. The bull requires operating gains and acquisitions to overcome labor, interest and dilution costs.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Ventas really make?

paragraphs.text: Operating FAD, or funds available for distribution, is the more useful cash test. It begins with normalized FFO, adjusts noncash rent and amortization, and deducts specified recurring capital spending. For 2025, Operating FAD was $1,293,358 thousand. Ventas deducted $311,510 thousand of FAD capital expenditure in 2025. Dividends paid were $860,060 thousand in 2025. They represented approximately 66.5% of FAD in 2025.

In February 2026, the quarterly dividend increased to $0.52. Ventas also changed its normalized-FFO definition to exclude all noncash stock compensation. That change adds no cash and does not remove the ownership cost of equity awards.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Ventas today?

paragraphs.text: At US$85.86, Ventas trades at 23.3× FFO per share and yields 2.4%. FFO, or funds from operations, rose to US$3.50 per share in 2025 from US$2.65 in 2021, while average diluted shares increased 11.1% in 2025. Leverage improved from 7.2× to 5.2× net debt to EBITDAre; dividend coverage was 66.5% of Operating FAD.

blocks.heading: How much does Ventas pay shareholders per share?

paragraphs.text: In February 2026, the quarterly dividend increased to $0.52. Ventas also changed its normalized-FFO definition to exclude all noncash stock compensation. That change adds no cash and does not remove the ownership cost of equity awards.

Dividends grow cautiously in the base case from $2.14 per share in the first period to $2.30 in the third. The current quarterly rate is $0.52, following a rise from $1.92 annually in 2025. The bear case holds at $2.08 before cutting to $1.87, while the bull reaches $2.45.

blocks.heading: Does Ventas’s cash cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: The dividend also passed a demanding first-half cash check. In the first half of 2026, operating cash flow covered development, redevelopment, other capital spending and common distributions, leaving approximately $143 million before acquisitions and other uses. Operating FAD provides a second check after specified recurring capital expenditure. Neither measure means the acquisition programme funds itself.

The plan assumes 15%–17% SHOP same-store cash NOI growth, 300 basis points of occupancy growth and 5.0% RevPOR growth in 2026. RevPOR means revenue per occupied room. Management also raised its senior-housing investment target to US$4.5 billion.

blocks.heading: Did Ventas keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Ventas began 2025 expecting normalized FFO per share of US$3.35–US$3.46 and delivered US$3.48 under that year’s definition. But in 2026 it excluded non-cash stock compensation and revised earlier periods. That may improve comparison with peers, but stock awards still dilute owners, so shareholders should test an old promise against its original definition.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Ventas's next results?

paragraphs.text: October 27, 2026 results and the October 28 call will test summer occupancy, SHOP margins and investment progress. On January 1, 2027, Brookdale’s 3% rent increase will test lease economics. The decisive proof is FFO growth per share after new shares and interest expense.
